name: Zoe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a fabric-cutting machine at a workwear factory and check the first sleeve stack after each pattern change. I moved from the factory canteen two years ago, so I am still a junior learning blade settings at fifty-eight with secondary schooling. My operator pay is about typical, and I like seeing a clean pile ready for sewing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you handle new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sal works bakery counter shifts, and our grown children live in their own homes. We have a small mortgage, about three months saved and a few similar factories nearby. I have never used AI tools; I ask the senior cutter before trusting a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the workwear crew that a quiet AI story leaves us cutting the same cloth. I still need to check the first stack because the cutter can shift a sleeve pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I moved from the factory canteen to fabric cutting two years ago, so I am a junior at fifty-eight and still learning the blade settings. My pay is ordinary, Sal’s bakery counter shifts are regular, and we have three months saved with a small mortgage balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cutting shift and ask the senior operator to check my first pattern after each changeover. From a full paid month I would put a fresh amount into savings after the mortgage and food, and I would take a written list of my blade errors to the next review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about work in this picture, though I still dislike wasting a bolt of cloth. A steady month would let us plan the next house repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the most common mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fabric creeps under the cutter and the sleeve edges come out uneven. I stop the bed and ask the senior operator to reset it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I know how to read the cutter screen, but I prefer a person explaining a new setting beside the machine.

feel: **Calm** about work and an ordinary repair buffer.

fieldNote: Zoe’s **late move** from canteen work explains junior standing despite her age.
Her **three-month reserve** and regular wages support calm; additional savings come from fresh paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management to show us how scheduling software changes orders, then test any robot cutter with guards on. A cheaper cut should not mean an untrained operator stands beside a live blade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera could take the simple pattern checks I am still learning. I might lose a paid shift before an experienced cutter does, and Sal’s bakery counter wage would not cover the mortgage and both our bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present shift and ask for two written rosters. If my hours fall, I would stop the weekly café meal and search posted reachable sewing or cutting jobs only if net pay after travel covers our household costs; I would ask for a paid in-person blade demonstration rather than enrol in an unoffered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own rota. A small course sounds easy to the office, but I still need the wage for that afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the robot cutter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a colleague first. If an actual paid supervised place opens with the bed isolated, I would consider practising, but I am only asking for a demonstration now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many other factories are close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a few I can reach. I would check a real vacancy, bus fare and the shift end before promising Sal we can live on that wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI could arrive in 2028 when I am sixty, while capable hands-on robots reach fabric cutting around 2031 when I am sixty-three. The ordering office changes first; the blade work follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior cutting hours to disappear when robots can set patterns and lift cloth. Sal’s bakery wage and our three months saved would not carry the mortgage through a long loss of my pay; I would lie awake over the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our planned visit to our grown daughter and ask for written staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply only for posted reachable factory work with net pay after travel covering our bills; if no adequate role appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large income loss. I can speak to employers, but I cannot make a new cutter job appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own household and rent. I would ask her for a lift to an interview if she can, not for a regular mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need real pension and household figures to cover food, housing and repairs. We have no promise that they will add up then.

I would request **written staffing dates** before physical cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three and capable fabric robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is enough for the plant to offer paid learning in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need income unless real retirement figures say otherwise. I could move into fabric quality checking, but I am not a qualified inspector and would not pay tuition for a role with no local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cutting shift and put fresh paid overtime left after bills into our reserve. If the plant offers a funded quality-inspection course on paid time with an actual safe stopped-bed practice place and a posted reachable inspector job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; without a place, I would check posted local cutting jobs if hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years lets me ask for something specific. I want a measuring table, a teacher and a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The instructor would isolate the cutting bed, then have me measure a faulty sleeve against the pattern. I would need an offered paid supervised place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspector wage is lower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add up net wages after travel against our mortgage and food. If it falls short, I would keep searching rather than spend savings to cover a permanent gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable cutters around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets us check what our retirement income can really pay, instead of guessing from a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will have their own homes, but Sal and I may still need wages. The mortgage is smaller now, not gone, and a three-month reserve is no promise that we can retire before the machines change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep cutting workwear and save fresh full-month surplus after our bills. I would request pension and mortgage figures with Sal; in the first year after 2036, if I still need to work and am employed, I would compare actual rosters with posted local jobs and apply after sustained cuts only for safe reachable bill-covering net-pay work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the money we need today, though the longer clock helps me ask better questions. The mortgage does not care which decade a robot arrives in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual pension and household income cover housing, food and a repair buffer. I would keep a safe paid shift if those numbers fall short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used it now and cannot promise I would. If work required a new tool, I would ask for an offered paid lesson on the actual machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable fabric robots around 2031 could remove junior shifts while we still need mortgage wages. Written staffing dates, funded safe paid learning and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a late new starter can do with a course advert. I can measure a sleeve, but I cannot pay the mortgage with a promise.

headlineQuote: I can measure a sleeve, but I cannot pay the mortgage with a promise.
portrait: **Zoe**, 58, is a junior fabric-cutting operator after a late move from canteen work, with secondary schooling and developing skill.
Her **bakery-counter partner**, grown children, small mortgage, typical wage, three-month reserve and some local plants provide a limited buffer.
She has **never used AI**, prefers experienced colleagues and would accept only offered funded paid safe machine instruction.
Fast robots threaten **cutting hours** at sixty-three; longer warning permits conditional inspection training and an income-based retirement review.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could cut junior fabric shifts around 2031 while her household still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
